At Fazenda Ponte Alta, visitors explore the history of the estate and its coffee-growing operations. According to the visit itinerary, the plantation was established by Baron de Mambucaba.

The estate's history is tied to enslaved labor: more than 500 enslaved people worked here. A visit provides an opportunity to consider this aspect of Brazil's coffee economy alongside the plantation's own history.

Fazenda Taquara is included in itineraries through the Coffee Valley. During a visit, guests learn about the history of the coffee estate and its main house.

The name Taquara is associated with the slender bamboo that once grew on the grounds. The itinerary tentatively dates the history of the main house to the 1830s; this date remains an estimate.

On Fernandina, dark lava stretches almost to the water's edge. A broad volcano rises beyond the shore, while cacti and mangroves grow among the rocks. The island lies in the western Galápagos archipelago, across the Bolívar Channel from Isabela. Here, the process by which volcanoes create land that plants and animals gradually colonize is especially apparent.

Cold ocean waters bring nutrients to Fernandina. Galápagos penguins and flightless cormorants live along its coast, while marine iguanas feed on algae. The shoreline rewards close observation: a lizard's dark body can blend into the lava, and a small bird may suddenly appear right by the water. Each encounter adds detail to the overall picture of the island.

The principal landing site on Fernandina, Punta Espinoza, allows visitors to walk among lava formations and observe coastal wildlife. The island is especially appealing to wildlife enthusiasts and lovers of volcanic landscapes. A stop on a western Galápagos cruise itinerary offers time to experience this part of the archipelago both from the sea and from shore.

The archipelago is volcanic in origin. Its natural areas and marine ecosystem have formed part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2001. Turtles, dolphins and many species of fish can be seen in the water.

On a longer journey through northeastern Brazil, Fernando de Noronha can be combined with Recife and Porto de Galinhas. It is best to set aside a separate stretch of the trip for the archipelago itself rather than fitting it into a crowded itinerary with several other destinations.
